title: SQL functions vs PL/pgSQL; procedures
summary: A simple LANGUAGE sql function is a named query the planner can inline; PL/pgSQL adds variables, loops and exceptions but is a black box to the planner; a procedure can COMMIT between batches. Push logic into the database when it saves round trips or must sit next to the data, not by default.

examples.title: One table function three ways: inlined SQL, VOLATILE SQL, PL/pgSQL

annotations.note: LANGUAGE sql, a single SELECT, STABLE, not STRICT, no SECURITY DEFINER and no SET clause: the planner can replace the call with the query itself, as it does for a view. This is a parameterized view.
The same body without a volatility label, so it defaults to VOLATILE. A volatile function may have side effects, so the planner must call it as written instead of merging it into the outer query.
PL/pgSQL functions are not inlined. The planner sees a function that returns a set of rows and, lacking a ROWS clause, assumes 1000 of them.
6 failed runs for test case 42. The other two functions return the same rows; only their plans differ.
Inlined: the function is gone from the plan. Its WHERE and the caller's status filter end up in one scan, and the index on test_case_id is used.

Function Scan: the function runs its own query, and the caller's filter is applied to whatever it returns (the Filter line sits on the Function Scan). Harmless for 40 rows; when the caller's condition is the selective one, it's the difference between using an index and not.

examples.title: String body vs SQL-standard body: what happens when the schema changes

annotations.note: A string body is validated at CREATE (check_function_bodies is on by default), then stored as text and parsed again when it runs. Nothing records that it uses test_runs.status.

The SQL-standard body (PG 14+, LANGUAGE sql only) is parsed once and stored as a parse tree, with dependencies on test_runs and the columns it reads. Dropping the table or the column, or changing the column's type, is now refused while the function exists.
The rename doesn't break the standard body: it refers to the column itself, not its name, exactly like a view.
pg_get_functiondef decompiles the stored tree, so the body already reads outcome. (substring keeps just the RETURN line; the full output starts with the schema-qualified function name.)
SQLSTATE 42703. The string body still says status and fails only when called, possibly long after the migration that broke it ran green.

examples.title: A procedure that commits between batches, and why CALL inside BEGIN can't

annotations.note: A procedure returns nothing (apart from OUT parameters) and is run with CALL, not SELECT. Unlike a function it may end the transaction it runs in, when CALL is a transaction of its own.
One batch is one data-modifying CTE (sql.subqueries-ctes.modifying): a run can't be deleted without being archived.
GET DIAGNOSTICS reads the row count of the last command; an empty batch ends the loop.

COMMIT makes the batch durable, releases its row locks and starts a new transaction automatically. A crash halfway leaves the earlier batches done, so the procedure must be safe to run again. This one is: it only moves runs that are still old.
Three NOTICEs, three committed transactions, one CALL: 299 runs were older than 2026-01-04, moved as 120 + 120 + 59.

SQLSTATE 2D000. Inside BEGIN the client owns the transaction, so the procedure may not commit it. That's also why this example uses sql-nontx: the sql runtime wraps the whole script in one transaction.

use_cases: Parameterized views: a STABLE SQL table function such as runs_of(case_id) that every client calls and the planner inlines
IMMUTABLE helpers for expression indexes, generated columns and CHECK constraints, e.g. normalizing a requirement code
An operation several applications must perform identically and atomically next to the data, such as closing a requirement only when all its test cases passed
Procedures for batched maintenance with COMMIT between batches: archiving, backfills, purges
Trigger functions, the most common job PL/pgSQL has (next lesson)
strengths: Unlike a Go or TS loop over query results, a function runs next to the data: 10,000 statements cost one round trip, not 10,000
STABLE SQL functions are inlined, so a reusable, named query costs nothing at runtime
SQL-standard bodies (PG 14) record their dependencies, so the database refuses schema changes that would break them; a query string in Go code gets no such check
A procedure can commit between batches, so one CALL can do a long cleanup without one long transaction
weaknesses: PL/pgSQL is a black box to the planner: no inlining, a fixed 1000-row estimate for set-returning functions, statements planned on first use and cached per session
Function bodies live outside the app's code review, debugger, tests and deploys; they change only through migrations, and app/schema version skew shows up at runtime
PL/pgSQL checks only syntax at CREATE: a misspelled table name fails on first call, not at deploy
Work done in functions runs on the database server, the component in the stack that is hardest to scale out

pitfalls.title: Forgetting the volatility label
pitfalls.detail: Functions default to VOLATILE. A volatile SQL table function isn't inlined, can't be used in an index condition, and is re-evaluated for every row. Label read-only functions STABLE and pure ones IMMUTABLE.

pitfalls.title: Labeling a function IMMUTABLE when it isn't
pitfalls.detail: IMMUTABLE allows the planner to fold the call to a constant and lets it into expression indexes. A function that reads a table, calls now() or depends on a setting is at most STABLE. Casting timestamptz to date depends on the TimeZone setting (the cast is STABLE); naming the zone explicitly makes it immutable. Otherwise cached plans go stale and an expression index can silently disagree with the data.
pitfalls.bad:
CREATE FUNCTION run_day(ts timestamptz) RETURNS date
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE
RETURN ts::date;  -- depends on the session's TimeZone

pitfalls.title: Row-by-row loops in PL/pgSQL
pitfalls.detail: A FOR loop that runs one UPDATE per row is the N+1 problem moved into the server. It beats doing the same from Go, but one set-based statement beats both.
pitfalls.good: UPDATE test_cases SET status = 'retest' WHERE requirement_id = 7;

pitfalls.title: EXCEPTION blocks as a habit
pitfalls.detail: Every block with an EXCEPTION clause runs as a subtransaction, which the docs call significantly more expensive to enter and exit. Catch where you handle the error; prefer ON CONFLICT over catching unique_violation.

pitfalls.title: SECURITY DEFINER without a pinned search_path
pitfalls.detail: A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with its owner's privileges. If its search_path includes a schema the caller can write to, the caller can shadow a table or function the body uses and run code as the owner. Set search_path on the function, with pg_temp last, and revoke EXECUTE from PUBLIC.

quiz.q: Which of these can the planner inline into the calling query?
options: A LANGUAGE sql set-returning function with one SELECT, marked STABLE
The same function without a volatility label
A PL/pgSQL function using RETURN QUERY
quiz.why: Example 1: only the STABLE SQL function disappears from the plan. VOLATILE (the default) and PL/pgSQL show up as Function Scan.

quiz.q: A procedure COMMITs inside a loop. Your Go code opens a transaction with BEGIN and runs CALL inside it. What happens?
options: It fails with invalid transaction termination
quiz.why: Transaction control is only allowed when CALL runs in its own transaction; inside a transaction block, the caller owns it.

quiz.q: You rename a column used by a function written with the SQL-standard body (`RETURN ...`). What happens to the function?
options: It fails the next time it's called
It keeps working, and its stored body shows the new name
quiz.why: The standard body is a stored parse tree that refers to the column, not its name. A string body would fail at its next call.

quiz.q: A function looks up a value in a reference table and returns it. Which volatility is correct?
quiz.why: It reads the database, so the result can change between statements: not IMMUTABLE. It doesn't modify anything and is consistent within a statement: STABLE.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: CREATE FUNCTION (SQL-standard body, SECURITY DEFINER, SET)
PostgreSQL docs: PL/pgSQL under the hood (plan caching)
PostgreSQL docs: Transaction Management in PL/pgSQL

body:
## Concept

Server-side code in PostgreSQL comes in three shapes:

- **SQL functions** (`LANGUAGE sql`) are one or more SQL statements; the last one's
  result is returned (all rows for `RETURNS SETOF` / `RETURNS TABLE`). A simple one is a
  named, parameterized query, and the planner can inline it like a view.
- **PL/pgSQL functions** add variables, `IF`, loops, `RAISE` and exception handling.
  Each SQL statement inside is prepared on first use and its plan cached for the session.
  The planner treats the function as a black box.
- **Procedures** (`CREATE PROCEDURE`, PG 11) are called with `CALL`, return nothing but
  `OUT` parameters, and may `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` when the `CALL` is a transaction of
  its own.

Every function has a **volatility** that the planner trusts: `VOLATILE` (the default:
anything goes, re-evaluated for every row), `STABLE` (no writes, same result for the same
arguments within one statement), `IMMUTABLE` (same result forever, so it may be folded at
plan time and used in index expressions). Getting it wrong costs either performance
(too loose) or correctness (too strict).

A SQL function body can be a string (`AS $$ ... $$`) or, since PG 14, SQL-standard
(`RETURN expr` or `BEGIN ATOMIC ... END`). The standard form is parsed once, stored as a
parse tree and tracked in the dependency graph, like a view.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java stored procedures via JDBC `CallableStatement`:** same idea, different call
  syntax. In PostgreSQL functions are called inside queries (`SELECT f(x)`,
  `FROM f(x)`), and only procedures use `CALL`.
- **C++ `inline` and `constexpr`:** a STABLE SQL function is inlined like an `inline`
  function; IMMUTABLE is close to `constexpr`: pure, so it may be evaluated once at plan
  time when its arguments are constants.
- **Go/TS query strings:** a string function body is like SQL in a Go string, checked
  only when it runs. The standard body is closer to sqlc-generated code: the schema is
  checked against it, and a breaking migration fails instead of the next request.
- **Python:** PL/pgSQL reads like Pascal or Ada. For heavier logic there are PL/Python
  (`plpython3u`) and others, but the `u` means untrusted: superuser only.

## How it works

Inlining is the planner replacing a function call with the function's query before
optimization. It applies only to `LANGUAGE sql` functions, and for set-returning ones
only when the body is a single `SELECT`, the function is `STABLE` or `IMMUTABLE`, not
`STRICT`, not `SECURITY DEFINER` and has no `SET` clause. The call must also sit in
`FROM`, without `WITH ORDINALITY`, and its arguments may not contain volatile functions
or subqueries. `EXPLAIN` shows the outcome: the function's name disappears from the plan.
The manual doesn't list these conditions; the planner's source does
(src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c, function inline_set_returning_function), and it
reads a `BEGIN ATOMIC` body as well as a string one. On PostgreSQL 18.7, example 1's
`runs_of` stopped being inlined (Function Scan again) when declared `STRICT`,
`SECURITY DEFINER` or with `SET work_mem`, or when called with `random()` in its
argument; a `BEGIN ATOMIC` copy of it was inlined.

PL/pgSQL is compiled to an instruction tree on its first call in each session, and each
SQL statement inside becomes a prepared statement the first time execution reaches it.
After a few executions the plan cache may switch to a generic plan that ignores the
current variable values. Two consequences: a mistake in a statement surfaces only when
that statement first runs, and table or column names can't be variables; for those you
build a string and run it with `EXECUTE ... USING`.

The examples use the single-statement `RETURN` form; a `BEGIN ATOMIC ... END` body holds
several statements and has the same dependency tracking. Its semicolons don't end the
`CREATE`: like psql, this sandbox's splitter counts `BEGIN` and `END` (and `CASE ... END`
inside them) only in a `CREATE FUNCTION` or `CREATE PROCEDURE` statement, so a plain
`BEGIN;` still starts a transaction.

## Design notes

Push logic into the database when it pays:

- **The work is data-heavy and set-based:** aggregations, bulk moves, batched
  maintenance. Shipping rows to the application and back is the expensive part.
- **Round trips dominate:** a multi-step operation per request that would otherwise
  be several statements with the application in between.
- **The rule must hold for every client** and you can enforce that, for example by
  granting the application role `EXECUTE` on a function instead of `UPDATE` on the table.

Keep it in the application when the logic branches on business rules that change often,
calls anything outside the database (HTTP, e-mail, queues: never from inside a
transaction), or needs logging, feature flags and unit tests with fakes. In TraceLite,
"coverage of a requirement" is a good SQL function or view; "notify the owner when
coverage drops" belongs in Go.

When you do write server-side code: prefer plain SQL over PL/pgSQL when one statement
can do it, use the SQL-standard body for new SQL functions, label volatility on every
function, and keep each function in a migration file next to the tables it reads, so
review and version control see it.
